articles.title_orig: Israel’s president picks Eisenkot over Netanyahu to form next government
articles.title_zh: Israel’s president picks Eisenkot over Netanyahu to form next government
articles.content_orig:
Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has tasked Gadi Eisenkot with forming the country’s next government, passing over the former army chief’s rival, Benjamin Netanyahu.
Herzog told Eisenkot of his decision on Saturday evening and will formally hand him the mandate at a ceremony on Sunday, the president’s spokesperson said.
Herzog held consultations with political parties this week to decide who he would appoint to form a government after neither side secured a majority in the October 27 general election.
Some 67 lawmakers, including from Arab-led parties, endorsed Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, to form the next government, while only 46 backed Netanyahu, the current prime minister.
Eisenkot will have 28 days – with a possible 14-day extension – to build a coalition of at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, the minimum threshold for a government.
In the October election, Eisenkot’s four-party alliance won 48 seats, while Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc secured 53, leaving both short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority. Arab-led parties, representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a record 19 seats.
Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties, which would give him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats.
He could also form a government with fewer than 61 seats if he wins a parliamentary confidence vote.
Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank on Herzog’s decision, said the president “took the predictable route” in selecting Eisenkot, as he had the highest number of recommendations.
“The hard work will begin now for Eisenkot to put together a government that can pass a vote of confidence at the Knesset that: one, will not break too many of the promises he made on the campaign trail; and two, that can survive the opposition of the right-wing bloc led by Netanyahu,” Odeh said.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government within the allotted time, Herzog will nominate another candidate. If the second nominee fails, a parliament majority can back a third candidate, who will be granted a final 14 days.
If, once again, no government is formed, a new election will be called within 90 days, with Netanyahu staying on as a caretaker prime minister.
Eisenkot led Israel’s military from 2015 to 2019 and sat as an observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet for the first eight months of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023.
Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Joint List – a coalition of Arab-led parties that holds 11 seats – told Al Jazeera on Saturday that Herzog’s decision was “expected”.
“We were concerned that the president would move towards a national unity government,” he said, referring to a proposed power-sharing agreement between Eisenkot and Netanyahu.
Instead, Arab-led parties endorsed Eisenkot for the mandate, granting him a “considerable margin”.
Tibi said he believes Eisenkot is headed for a minority government “with external support from the Arab parties”.
While this would not be a “dream government” for Arab-led parties, Tibi prioritised bringing down “the government of Netanyahu, [Itamar] Ben-Gvir and [Bezalel] Smotrich”.
Hours before Herzog’s decision, Netanyahu had warned that a government formed by the opposition bloc with support from Arab-led parties would lead to Israel’s collapse.
“Such a government, dependent on Islamists, will dismantle the state of Israel from within, as is happening in European countries, and far worse than that,” Netanyahu said in a prerecorded video speech, echoing the language of far-right politicians who falsely claim parts of Europe have come under Islamic law.
Netanyahu “described us as supporters of terrorists and terrorism”, Tibi said. “My response to him is this: Netanyahu is the biggest terrorist in Israel and the region, and the foremost supporter of terrorism, particularly Jewish terrorism in the West Bank and the Palestinian territories.”
Al Jazeera’s Odeh noted that although Eisenkot has expressly said he does not wish to form a government with Arab-led parties, “they both share quite compelling reasons to get rid of Netanyahu”.

articles.title_orig: King Charles would ‘carefully’ consider China visit
articles.title_zh: King Charles would ‘carefully’ consider China visit
articles.content_orig:
By REBECCA ENGLISH, ROYAL EDITOR and GLEN OWEN
Published: 18:29 EDT, 7 November 2026 | Updated: 18:59 EDT, 7 November 2026
King Charles would be prepared to undertake a controversial state visit to China if requested by Prime Minister Andy Burnham , sources indicated on Saturday.
As Charles is recovering from his 'challenging' Caribbean tour dominated by rows over slavery reparations, Buckingham Palace was not ruling out an even more politically testing trip to Beijing .
Such a visit would be the first by a British monarch to the communist country for 40 years, but would be fraught with controversy given the ongoing security threat posed by China to Britain. One Whitehall source told The Mail on Sunday: 'We understand the King would be quite up for it, if it came to it.'
But a senior Tory source said: 'This would be seen as seriously divisive politics.'
Royal insiders stress a trip isn't on the table yet and would come with 'complex' logistical and political issues to navigate.
As Prince of Wales, Charles made no secret of his antipathy to the Chinese regime. But a royal aide said: 'If the government said 'Will the King go to China?' I think we would think about it very carefully.
'China is a hugely important country... a very complex country. It would pose a lot of complexity in putting a programme together. This is the 40th anniversary of the last state visit.'
It comes amid a battle within the Government over whether to confront or appease Beijing. Security officials have complained that Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband is leading the 'appease' camp as the UK is so reliant on China for the supply of solar panels central to his Net Zero climate agenda.
King Charles III during his tour of Antigua and Barbuda. The Palace has not ruled the King travelling on a politically testing trip to Beijing
Prime Minister Andy Burnham. A battle is raging within the Government over whether to confront or appease Beijing
As heir to the throne, Charles maintained a highly–critical stance over the Chinese government, particularly as a result of his support for Tibet and the Dalai Lama. He boycotted UK state banquets for presidents Jiang Zemin in 1999 and Hu Jintao in 2005 over China's human rights record.
He once described Chinese officials as 'appalling old waxworks', and also wriggled out of a state banquet to honour president Xi Jinping in 2015.
Despite mounting evidence of state–sponsored activities in the UK, such as cyber attacks and political infiltration, Mr Miliband supports closer ties with China. One of his first moves as Foreign Secretary was to arrange to meet Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi.
Former Tory leader Iain Duncan Smith said: 'If it is true the King might be going to China it is utterly appalling. They are effectively at war with us, and should not be rewarded for it.'
Diplomats believe the King's Caribbean tour was a success, particularly his visit to Guyana, where he was welcomed with open arms at a time when China is making huge inroads in the region.
If rumours are correct, the King is to be wheeled out as Britain's version of 'panda diplomacy' and sent to Communist China.
Is this a state visit too far? I think it is. The issue is not Charles. He has shown himself a master of sensitive visits, whether to the US under erratic Donald Trump or to the Caribbean, where slavery reparations dominated discussion.
No, the question is: why are we debasing ourselves by offering a visit to a China leadership that behaves so destructively towards us? It would be ironic. The debate about historic slavery in the Caribbean pales against China's record of using forced labour now in its cotton and potentially other industries, including silicon used in solar panels that Net Zero fanatic Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband wants to cover the British countryside with. And we reward this with a state visit?
Too often our leaders, especially on the Left, continue the delusion that China is an economic El Dorado which will make us rich. But Beijing does not want free trade. It wants to make others dependent on it. This is not trade as a tool of joint prosperity but trade as a weapon in conflict.
Rather than organising a cringeworthy visit, our leaders' time would be better spent standing up for our values and interests and articulating them clearly.

articles.title_orig: New Zealand’s election results are too close to call
articles.title_zh: New Zealand’s election results are too close to call
articles.content_orig:
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

articles.title_orig: IRGC claims a self-imposed limit on ballistic missile range ‘has been lifted’
articles.title_zh: IRGC claims a self-imposed limit on ballistic missile range ‘has been lifted’
articles.content_orig:
Iran’s Revolutionary Guard says it has lifted a self-imposed limit of 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) on the range of its ballistic missiles, suggesting the country may seek to develop missiles capable of reaching more distant targets as fears of renewed all-out war rise.
Meanwhile, airstrikes near Yemen’s capital killed at least 27 people, according to a spokesman for Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry. In Israel, the president tapped opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot to form a government , in a post-election setback for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. Read our full coverage here .
The comments by the spokesman of Iran’s paramilitary Revolutionary Guard came days after the country’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khomeini , warned that “any kind and level of threat” from the U.S. or Israel would face a response without geographic limits.
Asked at a Tehran news conference about the limit on missile ranges, Gen. Hossein Mohebbi said, “That restriction has been lifted for us.”
Iran is not known to have missiles that can go beyond the 2,000-kilometer (1,200-mile) limit. However, U.S. officials have said technology from Iran’s space program can be repurposed to build intercontinental ballistic missiles.
U.S. Central Command said late Saturday it disabled a St. Kitts-flagged ship after it ignored multiple warnings and attempted to leave the region after visiting an Iranian port.
U.S. forces have been enforcing a naval blockade on Iran for months in and around the Strait of Hormuz , a crucial strategic waterway for global shipping, including of oil.
Iran established a chokehold on the strait at the beginning of the war, and has claimed attacks on tankers. On Saturday night, the Iranian military said two tankers in the area had hit mines and caught fire.
The U.S. says its blockade had redirected 144 commercial vessels through the end of October. U.S. Central Command also announced Saturday a new task force focusing on hampering Iran’s transportation options through its land borders and the Caspian Sea.
Iran state media also reported on Saturday evening the sound of two explosions on Qeshm Island in the strait, as well as several explosions in the port of Jask.
It wasn’t immediately clear what caused the explosions. U.S. Central Command didn’t immediately respond to an AP request for comment.
Airstrikes in a village near Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, killed at least 27 people and wounded 36 others, mostly women and children, on Saturday, said Anees al-Asbahi, a spokesman for Yemen’s Houthi-run Health Ministry.
The Associated Press could not independently verify the claims. The Houthi spokesman accused Saudi Arabia, whose Information Ministry did not immediately reply to an AP request for comment.
Since the summer, fighting has escalated between the Iranian-backed Houthis and their Saudi-backed opponents.
Israeli President Isaac Herzog said Saturday night that he was giving opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot the first opportunity to form a new government following elections on Oct. 27.
Eisenkot, a former military chief, ran as the main challenger to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, leading a bloc of parties seeking to oust Israel’s longest-serving premier. With neither his nor Netanyahu’s bloc winning a majority in parliament, the task to negotiate a coalition remains challenging in the deeply divided country reeling from the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attacks and the three years of wars that have followed in Gaza and beyond.
In the Gaza Strip, displaced families spent a sleepless night as heavy rain flooded their fragile tents, soaking mattresses and belongings, and turning camp pathways into pools of muddy water.
The rain marks the start of another difficult winter for the more than 1.6 million Palestinians living in tents or other makeshift shelters in the territory, where nearly the entire population has lost its homes during Israel’s campaign triggered by the Oct. 7 attacks.
The results of the U.S. midterm elections suggest that long-standing U.S. support for Israel is on rocky ground on both sides of the aisle. Democrats, who gained control of Congress , are fiercely divided, and many Republicans are increasingly critical of Israel’s government, particularly its wartime conduct in Gaza.
On Tuesday, as Americans went to the polls, President Donald Trump suggested cutting off aid to Israel . Then, a staunch critic of Israel, Abdul El-Sayed , became the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate.
The Democratic senator-elect from Michigan addressed U.S. Vice President JD Vance as “JD, habibi” — a common Arabic term of affection — in his victory speech. And Vance partly blamed the Republicans’ massive electoral losses across the country on U.S.-Israel relations, including the war in Iran the two countries launched jointly on Feb. 28.
This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

articles.title_zh: Pope Leo urges South America to bridge divides on Uruguay stop of 12-day tour
articles.content_orig:
The pontiff says he wants to bring a ‘message of hope’, as he returns to the continent that helped shape his priesthood
Pope Leo began an emotionally charged tour of South America on Friday, returning to a continent that helped shape his priesthood just three weeks after undergoing lung cancer surgery.
The 71-year-old head of the Catholic Church will visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru over 12 days in one of the most intense papal foreign trips in decades, meeting political leaders, prisoners, the poor, as well as old friends.
“I’m very happy to be here,” Leo told reporters on the plane before landing in Uruguay, saying he wanted to bring a “message of hope in today’s world”.

Black Friday is now just a few weeks away, taking place on Friday, November 27 in 2026. As always, this will be the best time of the year to shop for great deals, including popular Apple products like AirPods, iPad, Apple Watch, and more.
Note: MacRumors is an affiliate partner with some of these vendors. When you click a link and make a purchase, we may receive a small payment, which helps us keep the site running.
Specifically, in this article we're sharing all of the Apple products that currently have all-time low prices, or discounts that are at least close to their record-low prices. Of course, these are early Black Friday deals, so even better discounts could emerge later in the month, but if you're shopping right now these are all the best prices around.
You can use the links below to jump directly to the section you're shopping for today.
The Apple Watch Ultra 4 has dropped to $699.99 on Amazon in one of the most notable early Black Friday discounts, down from $799.00. This is a match of the all-time low price on the new Ultra 4, which just launched in September.
If you're shopping for a Milanese Loop model, Amazon also has a $99 discount on one of these devices. There are five regular models on sale and two Milanese Loop models, and most have delivery dates of early November on Amazon.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is framed as a legend retold. It opens on a tapestry depicting Hyrule’s people and places, as a narrator reflects on Link’s journey like it’s a valuable story worth passing down. For Zelda producers Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi, a desire to pass the original game down to a younger group of Zelda developers is one of the main reasons this remake exists:
“There are much younger developers who are working on this game, and I do think this is a really valuable experience for them to familiarize themselves first with the original Ocarina of Time and then have their own reinterpretation of it,” Aonuma said. “And to have those conversations throughout the course of development that may aid them in future projects as well.”
This is just one way the pair is reflecting on this franchise they’ve spent decades working on. I spoke to Aonuma and Fujibayashi for nearly an hour ahead of the release of Ocarina of Time, and we discussed the elements that make a Zelda game, how real-world inspirations and expertise play into game development at Nintendo, and their strongest memories and reflections as the Zelda franchise celebrates its 40th anniversary. Read on for my full conversation, including one of Aonuma’s key memories with Zelda creator Shigeru Miyamoto: "Hey, Mr. Aonuma, you know you can't really cut a wooden crate with a sword, right?"
IGN: It is great to meet you both. I'd like to start by congratulating you on tonight's launch of the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, as well as the 40th anniversary of The Legend of Zelda.
IGN: The opening cutscene of Ocarina of Time's remake and its tapestry present this remake as a legend being passed down. I can't help but think of the parallels with its development. Mr. Aonuma, you said that you wanted your team to understand the significance of Ocarina of Time. In a way, you're passing down a legend of your own, and I'm wondering if this connection was on your mind throughout development.
Eiji Aonuma: So the specific cutscene with the tapestry was not necessarily something that I had created with that in mind in terms of handing down a legacy, as you say. That was something that developers who were working more directly on the game contributed to. But for me, certainly as you mentioned, there are much younger developers who are working on this game, and I do think this is a really valuable experience for them to familiarize themselves first with the original Ocarina of Time and then have their own reinterpretation of it. And to have those conversations throughout the course of development that may aid them in future projects as well.
IGN: I'd like to ask about that more because one of my takeaways from this game is how much value I find in the traditional 3D Zelda formula, and you’ve said newer developers understanding the structure is one of the purposes of this remake. But it's also caused you both to revisit this traditional Zelda formula after several years away. Revisiting it with fresh eyes, what positive aspects of this more linear type of 3D Zelda have stuck out the most?
Hidemaro Fujibayashi: As you mentioned, Ocarina of Time perhaps could be described as simpler. And going back to Zelda as a whole, regardless of whether it's an old Zelda game like the initial original Zelda or newer ones, I think the core of what makes a Zelda game, from my experience and thinking, is that it's the combination of exploration and discovery. And that's something that has been with the Zelda series, starting from the very first Zelda game all the way to recent games like Tears of the Kingdom. And I think that's a common through line. And even as we’ve gotten into newer games that have the open-air gameplay style, it becomes a little bit more complex. But as we return to a more focused 3D Zelda experience, as you mentioned, it's kind of given us an opportunity to bring the comforts and the play styles of the modern games.
For example, having a second control analog stick so that you can control the camera. That really eases the experience of gameplay so that coming back to a more straightforward, focused experience really allows the player to focus on the core aspect of Zelda, which, again, is exploration and discovery. And so there's almost this multiplicative gameplay that allows you to dive even deeper into the idea of exploration, discovery. And that's something that I really felt like I kind of reconfirmed within myself that that is really what makes a Zelda game a Zelda game.
IGN: I'd love to know when this project started development. Mr. Aonuma, you've mentioned that this was a great way to celebrate Zelda's 40th anniversary. I'm wondering when the idea came up and if it was before or after Tears of the Kingdom was released.
Aonuma: It's hard to say exactly when the decision came about to remake Ocarina of Time in this way. I do believe it was after the Tears of Kingdom development had ended, we started to see staff being released to other projects that we were talking about the 40th anniversary timing coming up, and what would be best to celebrate an anniversary like this. So as we were discussing it and looking back over the Zelda franchise through the years, we talked about Ocarina of Time being a really good starting point for a lot of people who have played the franchise, and my professional starting point with the series as well. And I was really curious to see how the younger generation of developers at Nintendo would interpret a game like this for a new generation, for new players. So it's a little hard to nail down the exact timing because there were so many steps along the way, but I do believe it was after the development of Tears of the Kingdom had finished.
IGN: Mr. Fujibayashi, I noticed this was your first time serving as producer on a Zelda game after directing the last few. What was that transition like for you? Was it difficult to take a step back in any specific situations?
Fujibayashi: Even though my role on this title has been producer, I feel like my producer role has been relatively close to the front lines of development. But in terms of maybe a challenge that I faced was, because we now have a younger staff that's working with us, when I'm discussing things like what makes a Zelda or when I'm trying to provide advice or guidance, we have such a vast range of ages in our team. And some of the language we use or some of the way we communicate is a little bit different. So I found myself needing to adjust and recognize if this person has been involved with the series for a long time or if this person is new to the series. And adjusting the way I provide advice or, say, be involved with ideations with those people, I really felt like I had to kind of pull out my wisdom to make sure that the communication works for the person that I'm speaking to.
IGN: I've finished Ocarina of Time on Switch 2, and I really loved it. What struck me was the intertwining of these two eras that you've mentioned of modern presentation and controls through an old-school Zelda world. And I found this overlapping muscle memory of, originally I would expect Link to auto jump and he didn't and I fell. Or, I thought I could climb a rock and I couldn’t. My brain was pulling from Breath of the Wild and pulling from the original Ocarina of Time. What's something that sticks out to you about blending these two eras of Zelda together that makes this remake special?
Aonuma: There were certainly a lot of moments in development where our younger developers on the staff were considering how to familiarize and reinterpret the original Ocarina of Time. And we didn't tell them what to do in terms of “change this or don't change that,” but rather they would come to the experience and try to feel a natural need for something. articles.title_orig: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest
articles.title_zh: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and under house arrest
articles.content_orig:
Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago Peña over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment.
He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain.
Peña, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts.
He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests.
He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents.
Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing.
The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank.
Peña's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal.
"Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028.
The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank.
Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday.
An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, Asunción.
Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money.
Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd.
Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. One lawmaker was absent.
"It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," Peña said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system".
Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty".
Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history – a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image."
Analysts say Peña is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse.
His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".

articles.title_orig: GE Aerospace Reports US$12.9bn in China Agreements
articles.title_zh: GE Aerospace Reports US$12.9bn in China Agreements
articles.content_orig:
A global review of commercial flight
SHANGHAI — GE Aerospace said November 6 that it had signed sales and service agreements worth more than US$12.9bn at the China International Import Expo, including engines and long-term support for China Eastern Airlines (MU).
Reuters reported the aggregate value and scope of the agreements , citing a GE Aerospace statement. The total covers multiple sales and service arrangements, rather than the price of China Eastern's new-aircraft engines alone.
China Eastern will purchase 202 LEAP-1A engines for 101 Airbus A320neo-family aircraft, Reuters reported. A separate agreement covers 14 spare engines across the LEAP-1A, LEAP-1C and CFM56-7B models. GE Aerospace also reached supply and repair agreements with MTU Maintenance Zhuhai, according to the report.
CFM International's November 6 announcement confirms China Eastern's engine selection for 101 aircraft, together with spare engines and a long-term services agreement. CFM is a 50/50 joint venture between GE Aerospace and Safran Aircraft Engines.
The aircraft will include A320neo, A321neo and A321XLR models, CFM said, without providing an individual delivery schedule in its announcement. It says China Eastern already operates 215 A320neo and A321neo aircraft powered by LEAP-1A engines, making the selection an extension of an established engine fleet.
The airline also uses the LEAP-1B on Boeing 737 MAX aircraft and the LEAP-1C on COMAC C919s, according to CFM. These are distinct engine variants for different aircraft platforms; the spare-engine agreement spans both newer LEAP models and the older CFM56-7B.
MTU's Zhuhai facility description lists LEAP and CFM56 maintenance capabilities . Its separate Jinwan branch, operating since March 2025, focuses on Pratt & Whitney PW1100G-JM engines.
GE's latest financial results show the scale of the servicing opportunity. In its third-quarter results released October 20 , the company reported a commercial-services backlog exceeding US$170bn. Commercial Engines & Services revenue from services grew 17% year over year in the quarter; spare-parts revenue rose more than 20%.
CFM is also preparing for more LEAP maintenance as the installed fleet grows. Its July maintenance-network update described five-year investment commitments exceeding US$1bn by GE Aerospace and €1bn by Safran Aircraft Engines, alongside expansion of licensed maintenance providers and spare-parts inventories.
Those investments address the support needed after engines are delivered. For airlines, access to replacement engines, parts and repair slots can matter alongside the original purchase price. Airways has examined how engine-maintenance bills can remain elevated even as aircraft availability improves .
Neither CFM's announcement nor Reuters' account supplies a breakdown showing how the US$12.9bn total is divided between engine sales, spare engines and future maintenance.

Welcome back to Foreign Policy ’s Situation Report, where we’re back at full strength after our vacations to unpack the seismic U.S. midterm election results.
Here’s what’s on tap for the day: U.S. foes react to the GOP’s midterm wipeout , Ukrainians express hope over the results, and how Democrats plan to challenge Trump’s foreign policy in a new Congress .
Welcome back to Foreign Policy ’s Situation Report, where we’re back at full strength after our vacations to unpack the seismic U.S. midterm election results.
Here’s what’s on tap for the day: U.S. foes react to the GOP’s midterm wipeout , Ukrainians express hope over the results, and how Democrats plan to challenge Trump’s foreign policy in a new Congress .
Top U.S. adversaries are trying to read the tea leaves on what the Republican Party’s shellacking in the 2026 midterms means for U.S. President Donald Trump’s foreign policy moving forward.
Starting in January, congressional Democrats will have powerful tools to constrain Trump —and they’ve pledged to challenge him on issues ranging from the Iran war to Ukraine. But the U.S. president will still have immense authority over foreign-policy and national security decisions.
Along these lines, here’s how Iran, Russia, and China are interpreting the results so far.
Tehran gloats. Iran framed the historic GOP defeat as American voters rejecting Trump’s war against the country. “Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message,” Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrote in a post on X.
He’s right. As even U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance noted , the Iran war’s economic impact played a significant role in turning voters against Republicans nationwide.
Yet Tehran also doesn’t appear to anticipate any major shifts in U.S. policy toward Iran despite the fact that Democrats will soon control Congress. “If there are still those who entertain the slightest hope that the hegemonic system may change behavior or shifts in its political parties may bring about change, or that by making concessions to the US, they can persuade it to abandon its hostility, they’re gravely mistaken,,” Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei wrote in a post on X.
Though the U.S. carried out limited strikes on Iran in the days leading up to the midterms, Trump had pledged no major escalation until after the vote. International mediators such as Qatar have recently sought to rekindle diplomatic discussions between Tehran and Washington in the hope of reaching a deal and preventing another round of heavy fighting. Trump is now pondering his legacy, and it’s still unclear whether he’ll move to cut his losses and end the war or try to save face with a fresh military operation.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who is also facing a possible loss of power following national elections in his country, has reportedly been pressing Trump to return to war. But a majority of Americans now view the Israeli government unfavorably, and there’s growing bipartisan support for reassessing Washington’s ties with the country—all of which could factor into Trump’s next move regarding Iran.
An optimistic Kremlin. The midterms took place amid renewed efforts by the Trump administration to push for a Ukraine-Russia peace deal. The United States is poised to mediate talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi next week.
Trump has faced bipartisan criticism in Washington for his handling of this process, as the president has once again soured on continued support for Kyiv while moving to reduce financial constraints on Moscow. Though a Democratic-led Congress is poised to push for stronger U.S. backing for Ukraine, the Kremlin appears hopeful that Trump will continue with his recent approach to peace negotiations and relations with Russia.
“President Trump remains in office. We sincerely hope that he will continue his peacemaking efforts. There is already some groundwork in place. Another round of trilateral talks is coming up very soon. These include successful peacemaking and humanitarian initiatives. We hope that all of this will continue. Ultimately, this is an internal American matter,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told a Russian journalist regarding the midterm results.
China shrugs. Washington’s biggest economic and military rival is doing little to reveal its true feelings about the midterm power shift ahead of a prospective meeting between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen later this month. Asked about the election results on Wednesday and Thursday, respectively, Chinese foreign ministry spokespersons Mao Ning and Guo Jiakun had identical answers: “The U.S. midterm elections are a domestic affair. China stands ready to continue working with the U.S. to uphold and deliver on the important common understandings reached by the two heads of state, enhance communication, properly manage differences, expand cooperation, and build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity.”
Even the opinion page of the state-run Global Times newspaper, usually a reliable source of hot takes on U.S. politics and policy, has been conspicuously silent on the midterms save for one editorial that took a gratuitous swipe at Europe.
Trump’s desire for a meeting with North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un could also be impacted by the U.S. leader’s diminished political standing. North Korea conducted yet another series of missile tests the day after the midterms and appears uninterested in a possible meeting in Shenzhen between Trump and Kim, with Kim’s sister Kim Yo Jong slamming the United States as “hostile” and “unreasonable” in a statement on Wednesday and adding that North Korea had “no need to sit face-to-face” with Trump.
The midterm results—and the major role that the Iran war played in the election—have raised questions over whether Trump will move to oust Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Recent reports have suggested that Trump is asking political allies about this and considering making Hegseth the fall guy for failures in the war. Publicly, though, Trump continues to stand behind the Pentagon chief.
“I have every intention to keep him,” Trump said of Hegseth on Thursday. But the president also said he’s been receiving calls from people who are unhappy with Hegseth and doesn’t “understand why.”
But there are growing signs that Hegseth could soon face a House impeachment vote.
Meanwhile, former Army Secretary Dan Driscoll, who stepped down in September—reportedly over disagreements with Hegseth—has joined the tech giant OpenAI as senior counselor for national security modernization.
What should be high on your radar, if it isn’t already.
Ukraine’s cautious optimism. FP’s Sam Skove is reporting on the ground in Ukraine right now, where he spoke with Ukrainians about the U.S. midterm results. They expressed hope that Kyiv will receive more support from the United States with Democrats in control of Congress—but with winter on the horizon, they also have larger concerns closer to home. Read the full piece from Sam and FP’s Christina Lu here .
Democrats’ next moves. When the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, it won’t just be the Iran war that Democrats want to take action on. FP’s staff wrote a breakdown of the top foreign-policy priorities for Democrats after the midterms. Read it here .

Democrats’ historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could also have a dramatic effect on the tech industry.
In dozens of local ballot measures, voters rejected data centers . And even when they weren’t voting on the issue directly, they were electing politicians — like Texas’ new governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned on the promise of restricting data centers.
On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry. Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.”
And Kirsten said that while data centers probably weren’t the main cause of the “blue wave,” they’ve become an “an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about” getting their projects approved. And now, “we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, ‘Actually, we can change our policies.’”
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity.
Sean O’Kane: First off, let’s talk about the fact that one of the biggest data center builders was also the largest donor to the Republican Party. Elon Musk seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars — maybe even more, by the time we see the final count — and in fact is now sitting there with all of his businesses in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn for the first time in a very long time, if ever.
That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. But, there were also a bunch of ballot measures up around the country that would have paved the way for data centers to get built faster. Almost all of them got shot down, or voted against. [Actually, many of the ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those measures passed.]
With [Democrats] in power, there is a consensus view, at least in the tech world, that this is going to mean we have a lot of roadblocks ahead for data centers, especially in places like Texas, where [you have] folks like the governor-elect [Gina] Hinojosa, who has spoken pretty openly about this being a campaign promise and something that she wants to focus on once she takes power, now that she’s beaten Greg Abbott.
It’s the thing that I think the tech world is maybe a little too focused on. I’m curious what you guys think about that.
Anthony Ha: I don’t necessarily think that they’re too focused on it, but I understand why it would feel a little bit disproportionate — the data center ballot measures, certainly there were a number of them, but it wasn’t something that was on the ballot everywhere.
And in different races, the dynamic might have been a bit different, but there was this undercurrent and sense that it seems to be an issue that reaches across the country, that is bipartisan in a lot of ways, but that the Democrats seem to have been more effective at harnessing that energy. And of course, there’s all kinds of reasons why the Democrats did so well on Tuesday, but it does seem like anti-AI and especially anti-data center sentiment was a big part of it. That seems like a pretty potent political force.
The next two years, [and] potentially beyond that, are going to be more difficult for tech companies in general, and hyperscalers, data center companies in particular. I also imagine that they have to be a little bit worried about: Is this going to continue to be an issue, not just with the people who got elected this year, but potentially in 2028 and beyond?
Kirsten Korosec: Absolutely. I don’t think that the data center issue is what brought everyone to the polls and led to the quote-unquote “blue wave.” However, I will say that data centers have been an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about getting these data centers [approved] — very secretive, oftentimes requiring NDAs of a elected officials or appointed officials, not sharing information about the scale of a project in very environmentally sensitive areas, including in the Southwest, where there’s very much a water scarcity issue.
So I think that a lot of folks — Republicans, independents, and Democrats —  all saw this as wrong. They were motivated by it, but I don’t think it was a singular issue.
Now, here’s the interesting thing. There was a lot of waving of hands about how [AI companies] can’t possibly operate under any other circumstances. And we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, “Actually, we can change our policies.” They just released what they call a compute campus policy blueprint . And guess what? They’re not going to require NDAs anymore. They’re going to share their plans and supposedly operate in less secrecy.
I think what this shows is that when you put up either a regulatory certainty in the marketplace, or at least signals of going in that direction, then corporations will respond. If you don’t do that, they will not necessarily do the thing that we hope that they will do.
Anthony: One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase. So they’re not data centers anymore, they are compute campuses, and I’m curious, whether either of you think that’ll take.
Sean: I mean, this is ridiculous. Come on. It’s not going to change anything. It’s going to cause them more effort. For a company that likes to say that it’s no longer focused on side quests, OpenAI still loves to go in different directions a lot. And this is just the latest kind of thing where it’s just like: Why are you spending time on this at all? It doesn’t really seem like it’s going to move the needle.
Kirsten: I have a great idea for OpenAI. Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center.
Anthony: And if these are just lovely compute campuses, they should just build their own offices there or work next door, see how that works out for them.
Something else that I’m wondering about is, to what extent the election is maybe the second part of a one-two punch. [We’ve just seen] a big shift in how Wall Street is reacting to a lot of these hyperscalers and AI companies and this sense that [investors] are not excited about the idea that they should be spending all this money building new data centers, spending all this money on compute. And so there’s a financial incentive not to build all these data centers.
I’m very curious how that’s going to play out. [From a regulatory standpoint,] it’s probably going to be harder to build data centers. Wall Street is probably not going to reward you for building data centers. But at the same time, to get to the scale that they want to get to, they are probably going to need to build data centers somewhere.

articles.title_orig: French far-left presidential hopeful pledges ‘revolutionary’ remaking of society
articles.title_zh: French far-left presidential hopeful pledges ‘revolutionary’ remaking of society
articles.content_orig:
Hard-left French leader Jean-Luc Melenchon has been described as a “radical” by right-wing opponents, a “despot” by former allies and a “hero” by some of the students who have taken to the streets in nationwide protests .
The leader of the France Unbowed (LFI) party has emerged as the strongest contender on the left and potential challenger to far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen in next year’s presidential election.
On Saturday, Melenchon is presenting his programme at a rally in Le Bourget, north of Paris, a day after it was published online. Among his proposals, he wants to lower the retirement age to 60 and raise the minimum wage to 1,700 euro ($1,900) a month; pull France out of NATO and renationalise parts of the economy.
He wants France to stop paying back the debt it owes to the European Central Bank, effectively transforming it into a permanent interest-free loan – a move he hopes would give the government more room to spend.
On Europe, he envisions France remaining in the EU, but he wants to refuse rules that conflict with the nation’s social, environmental or economic programmes, setting up a potentially confrontational relationship with Brussels.
His party is gaining momentum as protests led by students in mid-September swelled to include several groups angry about failing public services, rising living costs and uncertain futures. The hard-left leader has been hailed at marches, some of which have seen vandalism and looting.
“His strength is that he is in tune with the demands of the demonstrations: better wages, money in education, a lot of welfare measures, no austerity cuts which appease people who are fed up with the cost of living,” said Jacques Reland, a senior research fellow at the Global Policy Institute. “He is the vote of the protesters.”
But some say his policies are radical and unrealistic.
France’s finances and borrowing are under scrutiny as its budget deficit and debt levels are high, raising further doubts on how Melenchon’s ambitious spending plans, particularly on social programmes and public investment, could be implemented. Some economists warn that his plans could cause investors to sell French government bonds, thereby increasing sovereign borrowing cost. “Borrowing money and deciding not to give it back – that’s called theft,” Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said in September, regarding such proposals.
LFI says higher taxes on wealthy individuals and corporations – another pillar of Melenchon’s campaign – would finance its spending plans. His proposals include a minimum 2 percent tax on the wealth of billionaires, restoring France’s wealth tax and increasing taxes on large inheritances. “Financial capital has benefitted, and it is the one that should pay,” he said in October.
His programme draws on a tradition of left-wing economic interventionism, rooted partly in Keynesian thought, that argues that the state should play an active role in the economy to correct market’s imbalances.
“Because this tradition of state intervention in economic and social affairs has been abandoned by most other political parties, the fact that LFI continues to define itself through such interventionism creates an impression of radicalism,” said political analyst Beligh Nabli, a professor of public law at UPEC-Paris XII. “Yet, this radicalism is only relative – it appears radical when compared to other contemporary political offerings, but from the perspective of the history of social democracy, it is not radical at all.”
Melenchon, 75, was born in Morocco to French parents. He moved to France as a child where he later graduated in philosophy and modern literature. In the 1980s, he joined the Socialist Party, but distanced himself from it when it shifted towards more liberal economics.
In 2008, he finally quit the Socialists and founded the Left Party, which would later evolve into LFI. The party appealed to working-class voters and marginalised communities and became popular with young people. According to this week’s polls, the presidential candidate is polling between 17.5 to 18 percent, widening the gap with his rivals in the left camp.
Trailing behind is Raphael Glucksmann, who leads the centre-left Place Publique party and secured the backing of the Socialist Party after winning a joint primary in October. Further back, and running on their own ticket – the Communist Party’s Fabien Roussel, Marine Tondelier’s Greens party and independent Francois Ruffin.
The left-wing bloc is undecided on the LFI. As Melenchon holds a significant lead, smaller parties are weighing whether to support him to give a left-wing alliance a better shot. Glucksmann has ruled that out, but others are pondering the situation. “This will be one of the key debates throughout the presidential campaign,” said Nabil.
Another source of tension across the French left is Melenchon’s strong support of Palestine. He has repeatedly refused to describe Hamas as a “terrorist organisation” and has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza – a term other left-wing politicians, including Glucksmann, have been reluctant to use. Melenchon has also faced accusations from political opponents on the left that his rhetoric fuels anti-Semitism, claims he rejects.
But Melenchon’s popularity is nowhere close to that of National Rally candidate Marine Le Pen. The far-right leader, who challenged President Emmanuel Macron in a second round in the past two elections, would easily win in a run-off against Melenchon, leading 70 percent to 30 percent, according to a Toluna Harris Interactive poll conducted in October.
Analysts say his economic programme is not the only obstacle. His combative political style and reputation for confrontation over compromise hinder his chances of broadening support beyond a core base.
“In France, it is often said that to win a presidential election, one must campaign from the centre. Yet, the defining characteristic of the LFI programme is that it is not centrist – that is precisely what makes it disruptive. He seeks victory, but not a victory from the centre,” Nabli said.
His leadership has also been criticised.
Several former allies have said their break with the party was driven by both Melenchon’s management style and political disagreements. Former LFI candidate Thomas Guenole has described the movement as a “dictatorship” governed by “an autocrat”, while former lawmaker Raquel Garrido said there was a left that agreed with LFI’s programme but not with the party leader’s “methods”. Former close ally Clementine Autain has likewise accused LFI of becoming “authoritarian”.
“He is the ‘supreme leader’,” said Reland at the Global Policy Institute. “The party is very organised, but it’s not a democratic party at all.”

articles.title_orig: Binance Says Kaiser Ng Leaving, Names Justin Yek New CFO
articles.title_zh: Binance Says Kaiser Ng Leaving, Names Justin Yek New CFO
articles.content_orig:
Binance said hackers used fake job interviews, malicious software and compromised internal AI tools to infiltrate its wallet infrastructure, leading to the record-breaking Oct. 29 cyberattack that resulted in more than $6 billion in assets being stolen from the world's largest crypto exchange.
The attackers "spent months building their way in," Binance co-CEO Richard Teng told CNBC's " Squawk on the Street " Tuesday, rejecting suggestions that there was a single point of failure through one employee's laptop.
"In June, [the attackers] set up a fake version of a developer tool and lured one of our engineers to install that," he added. "In September they posed as recruiters and ran a series of job interviews with another engineer, and that ended up in a coding exercise that contained hidden malware designed to evade security ... from there they moved violently through our internal AI tools and obtain[ed] access that breach[ed] the system that authorized our wallet transaction."
He also said Binance has replenished 98% of $6.34 billion in affected assets, and that it is still in the process of purchasing outstanding, more illiquid assets.
Teng himself did not attribute the attack to North Korea but acknowledged that the FBI has linked it to North Korean hackers tied to the TraderTraitor group.
Preparations for the attack began in June, when a Binance Wallet DevOps engineer downloaded a tampered Homebrew installation "to install a popular AI coding tool after searching for it on a search engine," according to a security report published by Binance Tuesday. It said it detected the suspicious activity, replaced the engineer's device and rotated credentials as a precaution, but that by then the employee's "role and his related colleagues on our wallet infrastructure team was exposed to the hacker."
As Binance works to recover from the incident, it has temporarily restricted certain withdrawals, pledged to cover all customer losses and tapped its own reserves to replenish affected assets. Binance and industry partners including Tether, Circle and Ripple have reportedly frozen about $3 billion in assets, though some stolen funds continue to move through laundered channels. Coinbase blocked transfers to compromised wallets and offered Binance direct assistance.
Although the incident represents a significant security breach, Binance maintains that it remains financially sound and focused on identifying the vulnerability, recovering remaining funds and preventing another attack.
The hack sparked a sharp but short-lived hit to confidence across crypto markets, especially compared with previous failures at major exchanges. Investors are now watching whether Binance can fully restore confidence in centralized exchanges.
As of Tuesday Binance has rebuilt the affected wallet system and internal AI tool, replaced compromised devices, decommissioned credentials and tokens associated with the affected engineers and expanded security scans across employee devices, Teng told "Squawk on the Street."
"We're also getting an independent expert to review everything that we have done, and we'll keep strengthening our defenses as the investigation continues," Teng said. "We're working around the clock with law enforcement agencies and with industry partners to trace and freeze the stolen funds for that front."

articles.title_orig: Berkshire Hathaway speeds up stock buybacks, though profit falls
articles.title_zh: Berkshire Hathaway speeds up stock buybacks, though profit falls
articles.content_orig:
Berkshire Hathaway said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.
The Greg Abel-led conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock. That's more than double the $4.5 billion repurchased in the second quarter and brings the company's total buybacks for 2026 to about $14.4 billion.
The sharp increase came as Berkshire's operating earnings — those from wholly-owned businesses — fell year over year, as profits from its insurance business pulled back.
Berkshire operating profits totaled $12.705 billion, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion in the year-earlier period. Insurance underwriting tumbled 43% year on year to $1.352 billion, while insurance investment income declined 14% to $2.734 billion. Berkshire's railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses all saw earnings grow year over year.
The company's overall earnings, which include Berkshire's sprawling stock market portfolio, also dropped 28% in the third quarter to $22.112 billion from $30.796 billion a year prior. Investment gains for the company fell nearly 50% to $9.407 billion.
Despite the earnings pullback, Berkshire stock has outperformed recently amid a massive rotation out of technology stocks. Class A shares are up more than 12% over the past month, while the S&P 500 has dropped 5.5% in that time. Year to date, Berkshire has gained 13%, while the broad market index is up just 7.8%.
Berkshire's five largest equity holdings remained the same in the third quarter: Alphabet , American Express , Apple , Bank of America and Coca-Cola .
Berkshire's cash hoard also grew 3% in the third quarter $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion in the second quarter. However, excluding rail and utility cash along with T-bill payables, the conglomerate's cash holdings totaled $352.3 billion, down 1.9% quarter over quarter.
— CNBC's Alex Crippen contributed reporting.

articles.title_zh: U.S. Treasury moves to cut off crypto exchange MEXC over $16 billion in alleged illicit flows
articles.content_orig:
Get The Block’s latest crypto news and price alerts for the coins you follow, right in Chrome. Add our free extension here.
On Friday, the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued an order against MEXC Global and said it was a money laundering concern.
The U.S. Treasury Department says it has severed crypto exchange MEXC Global from the United States after it allegedly supported $16 billion in transactions connected to Iran, North Korea, and Russia.
On Friday, the Treasury's Financial Crimes Enforcement Network issued an order against MEXC Global and said it was a money laundering concern.
"Financial institutions cannot have it both ways: Either you support the Iranian regime, or you have access to the U.S. financial system," said Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent in a statement. "Treasury will continue to sever the Iranian regime’s economic lifelines and thwart its desperate attempts to circumvent U.S. sanctions using digital assets."
Over the past year, Treasury has implemented a crackdown of sorts on crypto platforms allegedly helping Iran evade sanctions amid its ongoing war against the country. In June, Iran's largest crypto exchange, Nobitex, was sanctioned after Treasury said it processed more than half of Iran's crypto inflows in 2025. In September, the U.S. also sanctioned Iranian crypto exchange BitBank over alleged bitcoin transfers to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
On Friday, Treasury said that though MEXC Global said it maintained anti-money laundering and says it will block the use of people using it in countries including Iran and North Korea, that it had "severe deficiencies" in those AML controls. The department said Friday's sanction will protect the U.S. financial system.
"Today's action will protect the U.S. financial system from the significant illicit finance threats posed by MEXC Global," the department said.

articles.title_orig: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
articles.title_zh: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
articles.content_orig:
Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia , Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said .
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN , Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts , Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
after newsletter promotion
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.

articles.title_orig: A ‘Chaotic Race’ for the World’s Top Diplomat
articles.title_zh: A ‘Chaotic Race’ for the World’s Top Diplomat
articles.content_orig:
Meanwhile, Turkey's newly nominated Feridun Sinirlioğlu drew eight discouragement votes in his debut poll
Noushad Thekkayil/NurPhoto via Getty Images
Rebeca Grynspan, speaks during the opening ceremony of the 9th World Investment Forum (WIF 2026) in Doha, Qatar, on October 25, 2026.
Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan recorded another strong showing in the race for United Nations secretary-general on Thursday, increasing her support in the eighth Security Council straw poll, while Turkey’s newly nominated candidate struggled in his debut and the established front-runners maintained their positions.
Thursday’s straw poll again used undifferentiated ballots, concealing whether votes came from the five permanent, veto-wielding members — the U.S., United Kingdom, France, Russia and China — or the council’s 10 elected members. The selection process has also been shaped by informal regional rotation norms and calls for the U.N. to select its first female leader. The latest result shows that the newcomers took nothing from the front-runners, while Grynspan appears to be consolidating support.
Grynspan, a former Costa Rican vice president who would become the first woman and first Jewish person to lead the U.N. if selected, had her best day of the race, receiving 12 encouragement votes and three discouragement votes, according to reported results of the confidential ballot. Her showing improved from the previous round, when she received 11 encouragement votes and four discouragement votes.
However, the race is not yet settled as questions remain about whether she has overcome potential vetoes from permanent Security Council members. The last color-coded round, held Oct. 16, showed that Grynspan, International Atomic Agency head Rafael Grossi and Guyanese diplomat Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett had each drawn two discouragement votes from permanent members. Grynspan has since lowered her total discouragement count from five to three, but the latest results do not clarify whether any opposing permanent members have changed their stance.
The results also suggest that the entry of two Middle Eastern candidates has done little to disrupt the established front-runners. Feridun Sinirlioğlu, a former Turkish foreign minister and U.N. ambassador nominated by Ankara last week, received just three encouragement votes and eight discouragement votes, with four members expressing no opinion.
Sinirlioğlu’s nomination added diplomatic nuance to the race, given President Donald Trump’s relationship with Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, who remains highly critical of the Jewish state, and the administration’s efforts to defend Israel at the U.N. His initial straw poll preceded his scheduled town hall with the General Assembly on Friday and an informal dialogue with the Security Council on Monday.
Meanwhile, Lana Nusseibeh, the UAE’s former ambassador to the U.N., received seven encouragement votes, six discouragement votes and two “no opinion” votes — identical to her debut in the previous round.
Nusseibeh’s stagnant tally comes amid scrutiny over the UAE’s alleged support for the Rapid Support Forces, a paramilitary group accused of committing atrocities in Sudan’s civil war. The UAE has denied providing military aid to the group. Nusseibeh has condemned RSF atrocities, expressed support for U.N. accountability efforts and stressed that she would serve independently of the Emirati government if selected.
The controversy has intensified following a New York Times report detailing findings from a confidential U.N. report concerning the UAE’s alleged role in recruiting and deploying Colombian mercenaries to support the RSF in Sudan’s civil war.
In addition, an investigation by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies found an online campaign opposing Nusseibeh’s candidacy had ties to individuals with Sudanese and Turkish interests, though it did not establish that either government directed the effort. It remains unclear how heavily the controversies have weighed on Security Council assessments.

articles.title_orig: Russia upgrades Abu Dhabi delegation as Zelenskyy warns Trump's plan is dangerous
articles.title_zh: Russia upgrades Abu Dhabi delegation as Zelenskyy warns Trump's plan is dangerous
articles.content_orig:
KYIV, Ukraine — Kyrylo Budanov, the head of Ukraine's Presidential Office, expressed "restrained optimism" there could be progress made toward an eventual meeting between Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Vladimir Putin during trilateral negotiations next week.
Ukrainian, Russian and American delegations will meet in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10 and 11 for the first trilateral talks since February and the first since a heated back-and-forth over SpaceX's Starshield being throttled down . In an interview with CBS News on Friday, Budanov said the discussions would focus on postwar security guarantees for Ukraine and Russia.
"There are absolutely different situations at different times," Budanov said, referring to these trilateral discussions versus the ones in February. "Now, obviously, all parties wanted to hold this meeting. This means that there are certain prerequisites for this."
"These negotiations are not the last," he said.
Budanov, who led the country's Defense Intelligence service before taking over Ukraine's Presidential Office in January, will join the delegation led by Ukraine's top negotiator, Rustem Umerov. U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to represent Washington. Russia's delegation will be led by Vladimir Medinsky, a Vladimir Putin aide who headed Moscow's team in earlier rounds of negotiations.
"We look forward to building on the progress made in Kyiv, Oslo, and St. Petersburg toward a comprehensive, durable peace agreement that delivers lasting security for generations to come," Witkoff said in announcing the talks earlier this week.
The meeting follows several weeks of strain in the U.S.-Ukraine relationship. In October, President Trump announced a deal to allow Russia to supply diesel to the United States for the first time since 2022. Elon Musk's SpaceX also imposed limits on Ukraine's Starshield satellite networks, disrupting Ukrainian drone operations and some air-defense systems, before reinstating access weeks later.
Despite these developments, Budanov said he is optimistic about Ukraine's relationship with the United States heading into the trilateral meeting next week.
"Look, it's bad. It shouldn't be like that," Budanov said of the Starshield failures. "But along with that, we can remind you that this situation is resolved in one way or another. This gives optimism for the future."
The trilateral meeting comes as Russia intensifies strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Strikes this week hit energy facilities in 10 regions, according to Ukraine's energy ministry, left hundreds of thousands of households without electricity and cut water to much of Kyiv for more than 16 hours.
Budanov, speaking from his office in the capital, said Russia was using the strikes to create political pressure on Kyiv.
Russia's goal is "to cause the maximum damage to our critical infrastructure," he said. "What they hope to do is to create a foundation for social dissatisfaction, for street protests, and to stifle the national interests. But this will not happen."
