articles.title_orig: Son sounds alarm after father's medically assisted death in Canada: Way past appropriate'
articles.title_zh: Son sounds alarm after father's medically assisted death in Canada: Way past appropriate'
articles.content_orig:
Eric Edmeades recalls how his father's assisted death came sooner than expected and explains why he believes Canada's MAiD program has gone ‘way past appropriate.’
A Canadian man's decision to end his life through the country's medically assisted dying program left his son stunned by how quickly the process unfolded, and now he's warning that the system has gone "way past appropriate."
Eric Edmeades, founder of Speaker Nation, a training platform for speakers that teaches presentation skills and more, told Fox News Digital this week that his father Baz, who was in his late 70s and struggling with a combination of medical problems, began discussing Canada's Medical Assistance in Dying (MAiD) program after his health deteriorated in late 2023.
But what Edmeades expected to be a months-long process suddenly accelerated, leaving the family with little time to prepare.
I'M 25 WITH A TERMINAL DISEASE; WE NEED AN FDA COMMISSIONER THAT HEARS PEOPLE LIKE ME
Eric Edmeades with his father (Eric Edmeades)
Edmeades said the family started taking the issue seriously in January, but at that stage, projections were that it would take at least six months. He and his wife traveled to Vancouver at the beginning of 2024 to visit his father. At that stage, it was still a speculative thing that was months away.
"And then, all of a sudden, it was like, ‘No, it's next week,’" Edmeades recalled.
His father died via MAiD Feb. 27, 2024.
He had been experiencing a sharp decline in his physical health and independence, particularly during the COVID-era lockdowns, according to his son.
"He had been incredibly healthy most of his life," Edmeades said, describing a combination of symptoms that included epilepsy and neurological pain .
Edmeades also questioned whether interactions between his father's medications could have contributed to his deteriorating condition.
"When the lockdowns came along, and he could no longer go out and walk all the time, it really had a marked decrease in his physical ability and his sense of freedom and all that kind of stuff," he said.
"And then there just came this point where life started sounding pointless to him."
CATHOLIC NUNS SUE NEW YORK, SAY ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW FORCES THEM TO VIOLATE THEIR FAITH
Eric Edmeades with his father and family in Vancouver (Eric Edmeades)
Edmeades said his father had previously spoken about suicide, making his initial interest in medically assisted dying less surprising to the family.
"Given that it wasn't the first time that he talked about suicide in his life, it wasn't particularly shocking, but he also wasn't talking about it in really alarmist terms. So, I wasn't overly worried about it," he said.
Edmeades and his wife had already planned a trip to Vancouver and were able to spend time with his father before his death.
"And one of the things I'm incredibly grateful for is that I had incidentally booked a trip out to Vancouver, and my wife and I got to spend time with him," Edmeades recalled.
He thought he and his wife would have another opportunity to visit.
NEW YORK NUNS' CHALLENGE TO ASSISTED SUICIDE LAW IS ABOUT PROTECTING FREEDOM, LAWYER SAYS
Eric Edmeades with his dad (Eric Edmeades)
Edmeades said he was not in contact with his father's medical providers at the time and did not fully understand what had happened until afterward.
"It happened so quickly that I only really started to piece together what happened when it was done," he said.
Other family members and friends had also expressed concerns about his father's decision, according to Edmeades. He recalled that his brother openly opposed the decision and that one of his father's close friends spent approximately 45 minutes discussing the matter with him during his final days.
"At that stage, you know, for him, the decision was made," Edmeades said.
The experience has left Edmeades questioning whether Canada's assisted-dying program has adequate safeguards.
He acknowledged that there may be circumstances in which medically assisted dying is appropriate but argued that Canada's implementation has gone too far.
"What I see happening in Canada is way past appropriate," he said.
Edmeades also raised concerns about the government's role in overseeing the system, arguing that decisions about eligibility should be insulated from political influence and potential financial incentives.
"If I had to press a button and decide whether the MAiD program existed or didn't exist, I would say this," Edmeades said. "It should only ever exist if, and I mean if the process for approving people, it would be completely independent of government, and there could be no benefit to those people in making that preference in making that decision. Because otherwise there's a slippery slope, and we see that slippery slope."
According to the Government of Canada , individuals seeking medical assistance in dying (MAiD) must be at least 18 years old, capable of making their own medical decisions, and eligible for publicly funded healthcare.
They must also voluntarily request the procedure without outside pressure and provide informed consent. To qualify, applicants must have a serious, incurable illness, disease or disability, be experiencing an advanced and irreversible decline in their abilities and face persistent physical or psychological suffering they consider intolerable and that cannot be relieved in a way they find acceptable.
The government also announced legislation Oct. 27, 2026, that would allow advance requests while preventing the planned expansion of MAiD eligibility to people whose sole underlying medical condition is mental illness.
According to the BBC , Canada’s MAiD law, which legalized euthanasia in 2016, is responsible for one in every 20 deaths in Canada.
NEW YORK NUNS WILL NOT BE FORCED TO COMPLY WITH ASSISTED-SUICIDE LAW WHILE CASE PROGRESSES
Canada’s MAID law legalized euthanasia in 2016. (Artur Widak/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
A report from the Canadian Medical Association Journal covered by EWTN News claimed that implementing assisted suicide will "save" the Canadian healthcare system between $34.7 and $136.8 million per year. The study noted that patients and physicians should not consider costs when making such grave decisions.
In a statement to Fox News Digital, Ian McLeod, senior advisor for media relations and Conseiller principal for the Department of Justice Canada, said, "Canadian law is extremely clear: Medical assistance in dying (MAID) requires a voluntary request, freedom from external pressure and the person’s informed consent, among other stringent eligibility criteria and safeguards. Knowingly failing to comply with these eligibility criteria and safeguards is a criminal offense.
"In the current MAiD structure found in Canada’s Criminal Code, the mental illness exclusion is meant to exclude eligibility for MAiD on the basis of a mental illness, including suicidal ideation. The proposed amendment to the mental illness exclusion in Bill C-41, the proposed Medical Assistance in Dying Safeguards Act, which was introduced on October 27, 2026, is meant to reinforce this.
"This is why the bill reinforces that, in situations where a person has a mental illness and an eligible medical condition (e.g. physical or neurodegenerative illness), eligibility must be determined on the basis of the qualifying medical condition. A mental illness may contribute to a person’s suffering, but it cannot be the basis for determining that the MAiD eligibility criteria are met. Importantly, having a mental illness does not, in itself, make a person ineligible for MAiD."

Physician-assisted suicide is legal in 14 U.S. jurisdictions (13 states and Washington, D.C.). (Thomas Jansen-Lonnquist for The Washington Post)

articles.title_orig: Mass Effect 3’s Co-op Multiplayer Is Revived with Legendary Edition Multiplayer Mod on N7 Day, Even as BioWare’s Closure Hangs Over the Celebration
articles.title_zh: Mass Effect 3’s Co-op Multiplayer Is Revived with Legendary Edition Multiplayer Mod on N7 Day, Even as BioWare’s Closure Hangs Over the Celebration
articles.content_orig:
2026's N7 Day may be sad (albeit with a tinge of hope provided by a Canadian petition to the government ) for Mass Effect fans following BioWare 's closure, but the ME3Tweaks group (the same folks behind the Pinnacle Station and Happy Ending mods, for example) have a long-awaited gift in store for the community: Legendary Edition Multiplayer , now available for download on Nexus Mods .
As you can easily guess, it is the Mass Effect 3 multiplayer ported to 2021's Legendary Edition , which included the entire original trilogy but skipped the cooperative multiplayer mode that BioWare had introduced with the third installment.
In a blog post that Wccftech received in advance of the release, the modders go in depth into the making of this huge project. Codenamed ' Milan ', Legendary Edition Multiplayer took the ME3Tweaks group three years to make. In April 2026, the team decided to split it off entirely from the Legendary Edition; you'll still need to own LE, but the multiplayer mod won't otherwise interact with it in any way.
The mod, however, does not merely port the original mode for ME3; there are many improvements , including:
The ME3Tweaks group also made other internal changes to support future expansion of Legendary Edition Multiplayer, such as increasing the maximum number of supported maps from 30 to 255 . Indeed, they will release a mod maker for community use while continuing to work on additions such as the Redemption Map Pack and Rejection .
The former is a remake of the original map pack created by one of the group's members; the new version will feature proper lighting, pathing, and fewer networking issues . The modders also hope to add a brand new map with working cover. As for Rejection, it would also be a reimplementation of the original mod , which added several new enemies to multiplayer mode. The mod was prototyped but has not yet received a network playtest, and it may take a while to fix the inevitable issues.
The ME3Tweaks group has also done work to make creating new "kits" (character classes, essentially) much easier. Moreover, several minor improvements are already planned , such as improving in-game text chat, improving blind firing, replacing the Challenges interface and the downed UI, and enabling configuration of lobby sizes.
Lastly, the modders disclosed their use of AI , which had been nonexistent for the first two years of development. However, in the last few months, they leveraged AI tools for bug fixing, UI prototyping, pipeline performance, and feature research, which is pretty normal nowadays.
About the author : With over two decades of experience in gaming journalism, Alessio Palumbo has led the gaming vertical at Wccftech since August 2015. He started working at a young age for Italian websites like Everyeye.it, Gamestar.it, Nextgame.it, and Multiplayer.it before kickstarting the indie English-language publication Worlds Factory as its founder and Editor in Chief. 

In the last decade, he has coordinated the overall output of Wccftech's gaming section, managed PR relations, assigned reviews, produced daily news coverage, edited gaming content as needed, and delivered game reviews.  

Arguably, his trademark content is the long series of exclusive developer interviews that have been cited by Wikipedia and by the biggest news media and gaming publications. 

His passion for technology also makes him knowledgeable when it comes to gaming hardware and tech. His favorite genres include RPGs, MMORPGs, and action/adventure games.
Follow Wccftech on Google to get more of our news coverage in your feeds.

articles.title_orig: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits as AI Frontiers Group Is Declared Finished
articles.title_zh: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits as AI Frontiers Group Is Declared Finished
articles.content_orig:
John Langford, a partner researcher manager at Microsoft Research New York, has left Microsoft.
He declared the AI Frontiers group over, according to Digg , which summarised a post on his blog, Machine Learning (Theory). Langford announced the post on social media on Nov. 6.
The group had about 50 people. It was moved out of Microsoft Research and into Microsoft AI in early September.
Langford wrote that he found places for his team members as well as he could before leaving, Digg reported.
His account does not detail the group's formal status or where remaining staff were assigned.
Langford wrote that he and colleagues created AI Frontiers inside Microsoft Research in 2023. They wanted more organized research after the release of ChatGPT.
Much of the group's work centred on making AI agents function reliably.
Projects he named include Autogen, a framework for coordinating agents. Another is Fara, an agent that operates a computer to carry out tasks.
Shunyatax also described some researchers in the group as exploring ways to improve models without simply making them larger.
Langford described the leadership philosophy in Microsoft AI as focused on scaling rather than research, Digg reported. He said the environment focused mainly on getting, making and refining data.
He conceded the business logic. In his assessment, returns to scale are more predictable than returns to research. Still, he called a scaling-only approach misdirected and unenjoyable, Digg reported.
Those are his judgments. They concern the unit his group joined, not company-wide policy.
Shunyatax reported that Langford's position was not that scaling should stop. It said he argued scaling and fundamental research should run side by side.
Langford wrote that he could not get innovations used, or even seriously considered, while in Microsoft AI. A return to Microsoft Research held little appeal.
He doubted research could reach use from there either.
Langford wrote, in a post Digg summarised, that he is not comfortable being at a company where his research has no path to real use.
He added that there will be no internships with the group in the coming year. He wished well to the colleagues he is leaving behind, according to Digg.
His profile on the research platform alphaxiv lists him as a founding member of Microsoft Research New York. It also names him a co-creator of the Vowpal Wabbit machine-learning library.
A 2023 Test of Time Award at The Web Conference recognised his contextual-bandit paper on personalised news recommendation. The paper describes algorithms that learn which article to show a reader.
Shunyatax placed the AI Frontiers news alongside other senior changes at Microsoft.
It cited the planned departure of former LinkedIn chief executive Ryan Roslansky from his later responsibilities over the Office and Teams divisions.
It also cited the move of former AI platform head Eric Boyd to Anthropic.
The link is unproven. Shunyatax said the material does not establish that those changes stemmed from disagreements over research strategy, or that they are linked to Langford's exit.

articles.title_orig: Are hackers targeting America’s food supply?
articles.title_zh: Are hackers targeting America’s food supply?
articles.content_orig:
Acts of greyzone aggression aim to spread panic. Europe has to show the saboteurs that we are resilient
I t was as though a ghostly hand had switched the settings on supermarket freezers across Europe from “freeze” to “defrost”. From Finland to Ireland, they suddenly began heating up , many reaching 50C and food worth millions of euros had to be thrown away. But no actual hand was needed to cause the meltdown. This was a cyber-attack, or rather a chain of attacks. Like pretty much everything else in 2026, supermarket freezers are digitally enabled. That makes them smarter and more efficient, but like everything else that is connected to the internet, it also makes them more vulnerable.
Russian hacktivists claimed they were behind some of the supermarket sabotage, but no one knows for sure. It could also be Iran, Iranian proxies, North Korea – or unaffiliated bedroom hackers. When Transport for London suffered a devastating hack two years ago, the culprits turned out to be two British teenagers . Governments regularly warn retailers and other companies about cyber-attacks and even provide cyber-defence training to businesses . The lessons of costly ransomware and cyber-attacks also mean many big organisations and retailers have become much better at keeping their payments and logistics systems safe.
But freezers present a new vulnerability. In Sweden, for example, some of the stores that were attacked this week hadn’t connected their freezers to national retailers’ systems, which have centralised protection. Now they’ve learned their lesson the hard way.
Hybrid warfare – or, to use the defence term, greyzone aggression – refers to an array of hostile acts by a country’s adversaries that fall short of full-on military conflict. Cyber-hackers also this week attempted to meddle with fridges at French blood banks, while hoax bomb threats forced commercial airliners across Europe to divert, make emergency landings or require fighter jet escort to safety.
This comes after at least two years of sporadic Kremlin-suspected arson attacks on factories, explosives-laden drones flown into airports and drone incursions into countries’ airspace. There is constant GPS interference in the skies around the Baltic Sea, highly suspicious damage to subsea cables and pipelines, disinformation spread by bot farms and repeated acts of cyber-aggression.
Saboteurs and hackers usually have two aims: the first is to disrupt, but they also want to psychologically destabilise the target societies by spreading fear. It is fortunate then that the aviation hoaxes and freezer incidents coincide with a renewed conversation across Europe about resilience. It is as if the hackers wanted to showcase the need for preparedness projects such as the UK government’s new Be Ready campaign , which launched last month.
The British campaign, which instructs people on such things as stockpiling for emergencies whether caused by climate change or state-sponsored terrorism, had been in the works for months. Ministers hesitated however, fearing that citizens would respond with cynicism or ridicule, or just wouldn’t follow the advice.
Such campaigns are commonplace elsewhere. Earthquake zones such as Tokyo and San Francisco have had them for decades. “Make a Plan. Gather Supplies. Get Connected. Get Trained,” are the San Francisco city government’s pillars of instruction .
The newest version of Sweden’s official booklet In Case of Crisis or War , distributed to every home since 2018, is even more comprehensive, with clear language about everything from civil defence duties, how to volunteer (give blood or team up with neighbours for mutual support), to what items always to have at home, and how to find out if a crisis is real or a fake warning by bots.
For several years, I have been calling on the UK to follow Sweden’s lead and send a similar instruction leaflet to UK households, only to be told by officials that doing so would cause too much panic and frighten people. A House of Lords committee heard from the chair of the UK National Preparedness Commission in March that “the bulk of the UK population is blissfully unaware” of some of the risks they face.
It turns out that British people are less cynical than their leaders had assumed. Perhaps a few minds were also changed by Covid-19, which dramatically illustrated how vulnerable globalised and open societies are to all manner of threats.
after newsletter promotion
Either way, within a week of the Be Ready campaign launching, the retailer Robert Dyas reported that weekly sales of radios had shot up by 160%. Maplin reported that sales of radios had nearly doubled and sales of power banks had more than doubled, while torch sales had soared to nearly four times the usual figure.
The puddles of defrosted ice in the supermarket aisles and stress for air travellers this week show that we need to be prepared for a very wide range of threats including power and water outages. We have already seen what happens to our complex food supply chains when global shipping lanes are suddenly disrupted. Iran’s obstruction of the strait of Hormuz following US airstrikes has given us painful food inflation and costly global oil and fertiliser shortages.
But what if the ships importing the food we eat can no longer make it to our ports? No industrialised nation grows all the food it consumes. What if the internet goes down? It’s not impossible. Even companies with the best cyber defence could fall victim to sabotage of the subsea data cables that transmit nearly all our connectivity.
This week has been a nasty preview of what could happen in future with alarming regularity. Severe disruption will come our way so simply hoping for the best is not an option. The good news is that by accepting that we need to prepare, and demonstrating that we remain strong in times of crisis, we can signal to Vladimir Putin and other rogue actors that disrupting our services is unwelcome, but ultimately it is futile.
Elisabeth Braw is a Swedish security expert and the author of The Undersea War : The International Battle for Supremacy at the Bottom of the World

articles.title_orig: Berkshire Hathaway buys back $9.6 billion of its own stock but its profits declined
articles.title_zh: Berkshire Hathaway buys back $9.6 billion of its own stock but its profits declined
articles.content_orig:
Berkshire Hathaway said Saturday it accelerated its share repurchases during the third quarter, as operating and overall profits took a hit.
The Greg Abel-led conglomerate bought back $9.6 billion worth of Berkshire stock. That's more than double the $4.5 billion repurchased in the second quarter and brings the company's total buybacks for 2026 to about $14.4 billion.
The sharp increase came as Berkshire's operating earnings — those from wholly-owned businesses — fell year over year, as profits from its insurance business pulled back.
Berkshire operating profits totaled $12.705 billion, down 5.8% from $13.485 billion in the year-earlier period. Insurance underwriting tumbled 43% year on year to $1.352 billion, while insurance investment income declined 14% to $2.734 billion. Berkshire's railroad, energy and manufacturing businesses all saw earnings grow year over year.
The company's overall earnings, which include Berkshire's sprawling stock market portfolio, also dropped 28% in the third quarter to $22.112 billion from $30.796 billion a year prior. Investment gains for the company fell nearly 50% to $9.407 billion.
Despite the earnings pullback, Berkshire stock has outperformed recently amid a massive rotation out of technology stocks. Class A shares are up more than 12% over the past month, while the S&P 500 has dropped 5.5% in that time. Year to date, Berkshire has gained 13%, while the broad market index is up just 7.8%.
Berkshire's five largest equity holdings remained the same in the third quarter: Alphabet , American Express , Apple , Bank of America and Coca-Cola .
Berkshire's cash hoard also grew 3% in the third quarter $377.435 billion from $365.514 billion in the second quarter. However, excluding rail and utility cash along with T-bill payables, the conglomerate's cash holdings totaled $352.3 billion, down 1.9% quarter over quarter.
— CNBC's Alex Crippen contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Airstrikes kill more than 2 dozen people near Yemen’s capital, Houthis say
articles.title_zh: Airstrikes kill more than 2 dozen people near Yemen’s capital, Houthis say
articles.content_orig:
Media linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen say that at least 25 people, including women and children, have been killed in airstrikes by Saudi Arabia.
There has been no comment from the Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government in Yemen.
Live video footage on Al Masirah - a television station run by the Houthis - has shown rescuers pulling bodies out of the rubble of several buildings in al-Shariyah, a town to the east of the capital, Sanaa.
The bodies of young children can be seen among those dug out from the ruins.
The television station has also shown a number of injured people being carried on stretchers to hospital.
Saba news agency, which is also run by the Houthis, said the attack was carried out by Saudi Arabia.
The Saudis have led a coalition that has been fighting the Houthis for more than a decade in support of Yemen's internationally recognised government.
The war in Yemen had been dormant for several years but reignited as a result of the Iran war.
A truce began to fall apart when Saudi Arabia struck the airport in Sanaa - which is controlled by the Houthis - to prevent an Iranian plan landing there.
The Tehran-backed Houthis subsequently targeted Abha airport in Saudi Arabia, then began hitting Saudi ships that have been using the Red Sea off the coast of Yemen as an alternative oil export route to the Strait of Hormuz.
Major fighting has since resumed in Yemen between the Houthis and forces fighting for the Saudi-backed government of Yemen.
On Friday, an attack on a market in Taiz province, which has been the focus of much of the recent fighting, is reported to have killed 30 people.
The Houthis accused the Saudis of carrying out the strike, while government forces accused the Houthis of having fired a missile at the site.
The United Nations says more than 1,600 people have been killed and more than 300,000 displaced since fighting resumed.
The Saudis have regularly bombed Houthi positions, while the group has fired multiple missiles at targets inside Saudi Arabia, including airports and oil facilities.
Hours before the strike that hit al-Shariyah, the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted a missile heading towards Riyadh.
A Houthi leader, Mahdi al-Mashat, has vowed that the group will take revenge for the latest attacks in Yemen.

articles.title_zh: Ten Months of War to Gain 46 Square Miles: How Russia Is Failing on the Battlefield
articles.content_orig:
Russian Offensive Campaign Assessment
US officials are presenting a list of topics, including security guarantees and European security architecture, for upcoming negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, as issues that the United States, Europe, Ukraine, and Russia agree to discuss. Russia’s frequently reiterated positions on these topics, however, remain incompatible with the official positions and interests of the United States, Ukraine, and Europe. Former Senior Advisor to the US President Jared Kushner stated on November 5 that a US delegation held “productive” talks with Ukrainian, NATO, and European partners in Brussels to discuss security guarantees for Ukraine and the broader European security architecture as part of a lasting peace in Ukraine.[1] Kushner added that the United States is exploring five principal goals to address all parties’ security concerns through mutually agreed agreements: permanent security consultations, reliable crisis communications, greater military transparency, reciprocal measures to reduce escalation risks, and an enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.[2] Kushner stated that NATO will remain central to Europe’s collective defense and that each state will retain the authority to make decisions about its alliances–presumably referring to the rights of Ukraine to continue its aspirations to join NATO and of current NATO member states to remain part of the alliance. Kushner also noted that the United States aims to move to a broader multilateral negotiation format with direct European participation should the upcoming trilateral US-Ukrainian-Russian November 10-11 talks in Abu Dhabi make progress.
Russian demands for ending its war in Ukraine undermine wider US policy objectives relating to Europe’s defense and contradict Ukrainian and European negotiating positions. The Kremlin recently reiterated its 2021 demand that NATO roll back to its 1997 borders, contradicting Kushner’s statement about NATO’s role in Europe’s defense and individual states’ decision-making power about alliances.[3] This Russian demand also conflicts with US President Donald Trump’s ongoing efforts to establish a US Army base in Poland.[4] Moscow’s position on security guarantees for Ukraine has also long differed from that of Europe and Ukraine, with Russia repeatedly rejecting any possibility of the deployment of foreign forces to Ukraine and discussing having Russia and China involved in guaranteeing Ukraine’s security.[5] Kremlin officials have also revived their demand that European officials not be able to participate in negotiations to end the war so long as they refuse to negotiate on Russian terms.[6] Although US, European, Ukrainian, and Russian officials all seem to agree on the need to discuss the European security architecture as part of the peace settlement, the Russian position is incompatible with that of European and Ukrainian officials and with the requirements for establishing and maintaining durable peace both in Ukraine and Europe.
An unidentified actor is conducting a coordinated campaign of hoax bomb threats targeting European commercial flights, airports, and media outlets, likely to disrupt European society and impose economic costs. One or more unidentified actors issued bomb threats to at least 18 commercial planes and airports on November 6, bringing the total number of bomb threats against European aviation during the week of November 2 to over 50.[7] An anonymous senior broadcaster from Irish media outlet RTÉ stated that an unidentified actor issued bomb threats to 18 media organizations on November 6.[8] RTÉ, Irish media outlet Newstalk, Bulgarian media outlet Nova TV, and UK media outlet Sky News confirmed that they received threats.[9] A “Mikhail Andropov” signed the bomb threat message, titled “Message to the West,” sent to various European news outlets on November 6 and claimed responsibility for the previous hoax bomb threats against European commercial flights since November 2.[10] RTÉ and Newstalk stated that “Mikhail Andropov” claimed to be preparing a “new wave of attacks” over an unspecified period.[11] Reuters reported that it was unable to establish the sender’s identity, the email’s origin, or whether the email originated from the same source as the threats to any or all of the commercial planes affected during the week of November 2.[12] European security services effectively and promptly responded to the bomb threats, including by scrambling NATO aircraft to escort some of the threatened commercial planes, and did not find explosives in any of the targeted aircraft, airports, or newsrooms.[13]
European states have not yet attributed this coordinated campaign to a specific actor, but it advances the Kremlin’s military and cognitive campaigns against Europe and is consistent with Russian approaches, which ISW assessed in two papers published in September 2026. [14] European leaders, including Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares, Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto and Irish Taoiseach (head of the national government) Micheál Martin separately described the spate of recent bomb threats as “coordinated” in statements on November 5 and 6.[15] Irish Member of the European Parliament Barry Andrews stated “it is not a coincidence, in my mind, that this occurs days before Ireland hosts a major summit, hosting over 50 leaders,” noting that two informal EU summits are set to take place in Dublin, Ireland during the week of November 9.[16] European leaders should continue to prioritize attributing kinetic attacks and other threats to Russia or other responsible actors once they have gathered sufficient evidence to do so, as the German government did on September 1 following the Russian sabotage attack against Leipzig Halle airport on August 4.[17]
The Russian government continues to reduce its civil servants’ staffing level in order to cut non-essential social spending amid rising budget deficits. Russian State Duma sources told Russian business outlet RBK on November 5 that the State Duma will reduce its workforce by approximately 15 to 20 percent and that the Russian Federation Council will reduce its staff by approximately 10 to 15 percent.[18] Sources stated that the reduction of government staffing levels is aimed at reducing government spending and that there will be no “drastic cuts,” as Russian authorities will likely eliminate unstaffed positions and lay off retirement-age employees first. RBK noted that Russian authorities will shrink the State Duma and Federation Council based on Russian President Vladimir Putin’s October 2024 decree that calls for a reduction of at least 10 percent in civil servant numbers within some government agencies to pay bonuses to employees of relevant government agencies.[19] Moscow City Mayor Sergei Sobyanin in March 2026 similarly reduced the number of civil servants in Moscow City’s executive and administrative agencies by 15 percent due to Moscow City’s slowing budget revenue growth.[20] The State Duma and Federation Council staff cuts are the latest examples of the Kremlin’s ongoing efforts to cut non-essential social spending to direct more government funds toward Russia’s war efforts in Ukraine.[21]
We do not report in detail on Russian war crimes because these activities are well-covered in Western media and do not directly affect the military operations we are assessing and forecasting. We will continue to evaluate and report on the effects of these criminal activities on the Ukrainian military and the Ukrainian population and specifically on combat in Ukrainian urban areas. We utterly condemn Russian violations of the laws of armed conflict and the Geneva Conventions and crimes against humanity even though we do not describe them in these reports.

articles.title_orig: A Look Inside Jury Selection in U.S.S. Cole Bombing Case
articles.title_zh: A Look Inside Jury Selection in U.S.S. Cole Bombing Case
articles.content_orig:
Justice takes a painfully long time, but twenty-four years is an absolute eternity. When jury selection finally kicked off at the U.S. naval base in Cuba for the capital trial of Abd al-Rahim al-Nashiri, it marked a strange and heavy milestone. This is the very first death-penalty case handled by a military commission at GuantÃ¡namo Bay. If you think this process resembles a standard federal courtroom drama, you're missing the entire plot.
Al-Nashiri, accused of orchestrating the October 2000 bombing of the USS Cole that killed 17 American sailors, has been in U.S. custody since 2002. For over two decades, the case has bogged down in motions, appellate ping-pong, and profound legal battles over constitutional rights and torture. Now, military panels and defense attorneys find themselves operating in a legal twilight zone that tests the absolute limits of accountability.
You cannot understand this trial without looking at what happened before al-Nashiri ever set foot in a formal courtroom. Years ago, the defendant was subjected to CIA interrogation tactics that included waterboarding and mock executions. Those severe abuses created a massive hurdle for prosecutors.
Back in 2023, the military judge threw out confessions al-Nashiri made to investigators because those statements were fundamentally tainted by prior torture. That single ruling stripped the government of its primary direct evidence. Prosecutors have to build a capital case without the confessions that investigators spent years gathering. That forces a heavy reliance on circumstantial evidence, foreign intelligence sharing, and testimony from aging witnesses who remember an attack that happened a quarter-century ago.
Just days before prospective military jurors boarded flights to Cuba, the entire proceeding nearly ground to a halt over sanity questions. Defense forensic psychiatrists argued that decades of abuse left al-Nashiri with a traumatic brain injury and severe neurocognitive disorders, rendering him mentally incompetent to stand trial.
Army Colonel Matthew Fitzgerald, the presiding judge, ordered a sanity board evaluation. The resulting decision ruled that the defense failed to overcome the legal presumption of competence, clearing the path for the 36-member military pool to begin the painstaking process of vetting jurors. Even so, mental health appeals will likely form the bedrock of any future post-conviction challenges.
Normal federal courts handle terrorism trials with established constitutional protections, open public access, and clear precedents. GuantÃ¡namo military commissions operate under a separate, hybrid framework created specifically for war crimes and alien unprivileged enemy combatants.
Legal experts have criticized this parallel system from day one. Critics argue that ad-hoc military tribunals create an appearance of a rigged outcome, whereas supporters insist they provide necessary security and flexibility for prosecuting acts of war outside standard domestic jurisdictions. When a trial takes nearly a quarter of a century to reach a jury, public confidence takes a massive hit regardless of the verdict.
Selecting a jury for a capital case is notoriously grueling under any circumstances. Doing it with active-duty military members serving as jurors on a remote island base introduces logistics you won't find anywhere else. The proceedings will happen in structured windows, keeping press and observers restricted by tight military flight schedules.
The legal teams will spend weeks questioning service members about command influence, bias, and their knowledge of the case. Every single ruling handed down right now establishes precedents that will haunt military law for generations. This isn't just about one man or one tragic bombing. It's a live stress test of whether a military commission can ever deliver credible justice after decades of institutional delays and torture controversies.
Elena Coleman is a prolific writer and researcher with expertise in digital media, emerging technologies, and social trends shaping the modern world.

articles.title_zh: To Cross the Red Sea, Shippers Email Houthi Rebels. Read Their Inbox.
articles.content_orig:
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute are publishing updates Monday through Friday to provide analysis on the war with Iran and the broader Middle East. Weekday updates cover events from the past 24-hour period, whereas weekend updates are abbreviated and cover the Houthi-Saudi conflict and major breaking developments related to the war with Iran.
The Houthi-controlled Humanitarian Operations Coordination Center (HOCC) has reportedly issued voluntary "transit permits" in recent months that grant civilian vessels safe passage through the Bab al Mandeb Strait. The Houthis’ establishment of a permit system sets conditions for the Houthis to exert greater control over maritime traffic through the strait in the future by normalizing the Houthis’ regulation of shipping through the waterway. The Wall Street Journal reported on November 6 that "some" civilian cargo vessels have coordinated with the HOCC to secure voluntary "transit permits" in order to minimize the risk of Houthi attacks. [i] The HOCC previously announced on August 1 that the Houthis would only allow "authorized" civilian vessels to transit through the strait and the Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi vessels to enforce their blockade on Saudi Arabia. [ii] The HOCC, which the Houthis have used since 2024 to communicate with international shipping companies, closely resembles the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, which Iran established in May 2026 to regulate traffic through the Strait of Hormuz. [iii]
The Wall Street Journal reported that "many" vessels have not contacted the HOCC as they transit the strait due to the United States' designation of the Houthis as a Foreign Terrorist Organization. [iv] The Houthis could at any time choose to compel international civilian vessels to acquire mandatory transit permits and enforce their decision by striking vessels in the Red Sea and Bab al Mandeb that refuse to coordinate with the HOCC. The Houthis have established control over territory along Yemen's Red Sea coast since September 10, which puts Houthi forces at a closer range from which they can target international shipping. [v] Iran has implemented a similar mandatory transit permit system and fees for maritime traffic transiting through the Strait of Hormuz, which the regime has attempted to enforce through repeated attacks on civilian shipping. [vi]
Allowing state and non-state actors to control transit through global chokepoints risks causing economic disruption for the United States and its partners over the long term. Iranian and Houthi control over the Strait of Hormuz and Bab al Mandeb Strait, respectively, causes economic disruption by increasing insurance rates, raising shipping costs, and imposing transit fees:
International shipping costs do not typically return to pre-crisis levels once a crisis has ended, particularly if a state or non-state actor retains the ability to resume its restrictions under threat of force. The average global cost to ship a standard 40-foot container has increased from $1,899 USD near the start of the Iran War in late February 2026 to $4,389 USD as of November 5. [xv] The average global container shipping cost peaked in early July 2026 and has remained above $4,200 USD through November 2026, which, at least in part, is likely due to the start of the Houthi blockade against Saudi Arabia on July 20 and Iran's ongoing strikes on civilian vessels in the Strait of Hormuz. [xvi] The Houthis had a similar effect on global shipping prices between 2023 and 2025, as prices remained elevated over the two-year period even after the Houthis largely halted strikes on civilian vessels in November 2024. [xvii]
The Houthis may be concentrating forces and materiel in al Turbah, which lies astride the Taiz-Aden ground line of communication (GLOC), in preparation for a large-scale offensive operation into Lahij Governorate and toward Aden. An independent Yemeni journalist reported on November 5 that the Houthis have moved military equipment from rural areas on the Taiz-Lahij governorate border to al Turbah in southeastern Taiz Governorate. [xviii] The journalist reported that the equipment transfers occurred during a period of relatively low kinetic activity on the frontlines along the GLOC in Maqatirah District, southeast of al Turbah. [xix] Another Yemeni journalist reported on November 5 that Saudi forces conducted airstrikes on Houthi fighters and vehicles in al Turbah. [xx] These reports suggest that the Houthis may be concentrating forces and supplies in al Turbah amid ongoing Houthi efforts to advance southeastward along the GLOC and threaten the Yemeni government's de facto capital in Aden. [xxi]
Al Turbah is an ideal staging area for a Houthi offensive southeastward into Maqatirah District along and around the Taiz-Aden GLOC. Al Turbah is the largest town in southeastern Taiz Governorate and lies in the Houthi rear several kilometers behind the current frontlines in Maqatirah District. The town's location on the Taiz-Aden GLOC enables the Houthis to receive and assemble reinforcements and supplies from Houthi-controlled territory further north, and its position at a key junction in the GLOC could enable simultaneous Houthi advances along the roadway's southern and eastern forks into Maqatirah District. [xxii] The Houthis could also attempt to exploit smaller, less developed roadways that extend south from al Turbah to infiltrate government-held territory in valleys southwest of the GLOC. [xxiii] The Houthis have likely used these roadways to infiltrate areas surrounding al Majza, about 25 kilometers southwest of the GLOC, in recent days to divert Yemeni government-aligned forces defending positions along the GLOC. [xxiv]
A concentrated Houthi offensive along the Taiz-Aden GLOC in northern Lahij Governorate would likely encounter vulnerabilities and challenges from local terrain and Yemeni government-aligned forces, however. The rugged mountain valley terrain in Taiz and Lahij governorates generally forces large, vehicle-dependent military columns to use the few available local roadways. [xxv] These roadways, even the Taiz-Aden GLOC, are relatively narrow and poorly maintained, which would require large Houthi vehicle columns to advance slowly and single-file. [xxvi] Local Yemeni government-aligned forces' knowledge of the rugged terrain could help them ambush these columns and identify targets for close air support (CAS). [xxvii] Yemeni government-aligned forces demonstrated their ability to coordinate effective CAS with Saudi aircraft on October 30, when Saudi airstrikes destroyed a Houthi vehicle column attempting to advance along the GLOC at Hayjat al Abd. [xxviii]
Iran may have deployed at least four commercial vessels to map subsea cable routes in the Gulf of Oman last month. Iran would need to conduct such reconnaissance before conducting any operation to disrupt and damage regional subsea cables, which Iranian officials have recently threatened to do if the United States and Israel conduct strikes on Iran. A shipping analytics firm recorded suspicious movements by three US-sanctioned vessels in the Gulf of Oman and an Iranian fishing vessel over the Europe-India Gateway cable south of Oman between October 21 and 26. [xxix] Their movements reportedly matched patterns commonly associated with subsea cable mapping, according to the firm speaking to the Financial Times on November 6. [xxx] Iranian officials, including Supreme National Security Council Secretary Major General Mohsen Rezaei, have threatened to attack subsea cables in the Persian Gulf in recent months if the United States resumes airstrikes against Iran. [xxxi] Iran would need to map subsea cable routes before conducting any operation to disrupt them, given that publicly available maps of subsea cable systems only show approximate locations of the systems. articles.title_orig: Democrats Just Swept Congress — and 80 Years of Stock Market History Says This Happens Next - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: Democrats Just Swept Congress — and 80 Years of Stock Market History Says This Happens Next - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
Eighty years of midterm history say stocks usually thrive after a divided Congress, yet Wall Street panicked within days. One crowded corner of the market could break a streak that has never failed, and three signals will show which way…
This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them.
Voters handed Democrats both the House and the Senate in the November 3 midterms, so President Donald Trump will govern with a divided Congress starting in January 2027. Wall Street liked the result at first: the Dow posted its biggest gain of the year the next day. Then the mood turned. The tech-heavy index plunged 5.56% on November 5 as investors began pricing in tighter regulation of AI infrastructure . The VIX , Wall Street’s fear gauge, rose to 28.18 from 16.61 a session earlier.
That swing raises a question for investors. Eighty years of midterm history point to a good year ahead for stocks. This cycle could still test that record because so much of the market now rides on one theme.
The S&P 500 has risen in all 20 completed 12-month periods after midterm elections since 1946, gaining 14.7% on average. Divided government barely changes that. In 16 of the 21 midterms since 1946, voters sent the president a Congress controlled by the other party. The average 12-month return was 14.6% under divided government and 14.9% under unified government.
Today’s setup has the best record of all. The nine instances of a Democratic Congress combined with a Republican president produced an average S&P 500 gain of 16.2% over the following year. Gridlock means fewer policy shocks, a point Reuters reported traders were cheering right after the results.
AI-related companies now make up more than 30% of the S&P 500, and Democrats may push for tighter regulation of how much electricity and water data centers use. That pressure is building on its own. The Department of Energy projects data centers could account for up to 12% of U.S. electrical demand by 2028. PJM Interconnection’s independent market monitor called data center load growth “the primary reason” for tight supply and high capacity prices on its grid. Even without passing a law, a Congress with committee control can slow permitting through hearings alone.
Investors are already sorting winners from losers. From election day through November 6, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:SPY ) fell 2.53% while the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust ( NYSEARCA:DIA ) slid just 0.94%. The tech-heavy Invesco QQQ Trust ( NASDAQ:QQQ ) is down 13.41% over the past month.
Who controls Congress is just one factor among many. The economy grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter. The 10-year Treasury yield has fallen to 4.84% from 5.24% in early October, which helps growth-stock valuations. The Fed’s target rate is capped at 4.00%. Households are the weak spot: University of Michigan consumer sentiment fell to 48.1 in September, below the index’s recession threshold.
Keep the history in perspective. The samples are small, and returns ultimately come down to earnings, interest rates and valuations.
For a diversified portfolio, the Democratic sweep has historically been a good setup. The exposure worth a closer look is concentration in AI. Three signals matter most over the next two quarters:

For the past 20 years, he’s been cruising the markets looking for companies to lock up as long-term holdings in a portfolio while writing extensively on the broad sectors of consumer goods, technology, and industrials. Because his experience isn’t from the typical financial analyst track, Rich is able to break down complex topics into understandable and useful action points for the average investor. articles.title_orig: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.title_zh: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
articles.content_orig:
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests, on 5.
The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te Pāti Māori, which represents Māori interests.
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens – who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops – saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices – for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

articles.title_zh: Stellar Blade Nintendo Switch 2 tech analysis, including frame rate and resolution
articles.content_orig:
Stellar Blade came to Nintendo Switch 2 this week, and thanks to Digital Foundry, we have various technical details covering frame rate, resolution, and more.
Stellar Blade is one of the first games on the console to use frame generation, which is one of the things discussed here. We also have information about changes and cutbacks compared to the PS5 version.
Here’s the full roundup of tidbits:
– Switch 2 strips back environmental detail compared to PS5 – Pop-in is also more of a concern – In some shots, the cutbacks are less apparent – Details cut back more aggressively in larger scale shots – Lighting cutbacks as well – DLSS used on Switch 2 for a more stable presentation than PS5 – Switch 2 docked resolution is about 540p internally – Uses FSR3 frame generation by default on Switch 2 to take 30 FPS input to 60 FPS – Exploration usually better at hitting and holding 60 FPS for healthy periods – This isn’t done as often during combat and cutscenes with dropped frames – Extended dips don’t happen too often – With frame generation off, the game looks basically identical – With it off, internal docked resolution is about 648p – You’ll get a frame rate of about 35-45 FPS with it off – Handheld resolution is about 360p internally – Performance is similar with handheld and docked modes – In handheld mode with frame gen off, VRR helps with frame rate

articles.title_orig: 31-year-old dumpster diver brought in $140,000 in 12 months: I 'did much more than I thought was possible'
articles.title_zh: 31-year-old dumpster diver brought in $140,000 in 12 months: I 'did much more than I thought was possible'
articles.content_orig:
When Carter Stevens tells people he makes six figures a year digging through dumpsters, they often assume he's "blowing smoke," he says.
Not everyone sees dollar signs in a brimming dumpster. But Stevens earned roughly $140,000 in total sales between September 2025 and September 2026 by salvaging trashed items, cleaning them up and selling them on platforms like eBay and Facebook Marketplace, according to documents reviewed by CNBC Make It.
Stevens primarily operates near office parks and luxury condominiums around Nashville, Tennessee. Since March 2024, when he started dumpster diving, he's found and sold hand-crafted Persian rugs, high-end office chairs and even samurai swords, he says. Trash-picking helps him keep his shipping costs low, he adds: Some of his supplies, like cardboard boxes and packing tape, also come from dumpsters, enough that he doesn't have to pay for them approximately "90% of the time."
"The amount of waste in this country that you'll find is unbelievable. We throw so much stuff out," says Stevens, 31.
Sometimes, Stevens asks a building for permission to go through its trash, marketing himself as a junk removal service. In that way, his job is similar — though not identical, because he generally only takes what he can sell, he says — to other entrepreneurs across the U.S. who follow advice in Reddit threads or YouTube tutorials to launch junk removal side hustles or full-time businesses . There are around 10,000 junk removal businesses across the U.S., according to the Better Business Bureau. They range in scale from independent side hustles to national companies like 1-800-GOT-JUNK , which touts more than 150 franchise locations.
Other times, Stevens finds himself neck deep in rubbish, ducking concerned security guards, peeling away actual trash and rotting food in the hope of uncovering discarded treasure, he says. He tries to avoid sneaking around and keeps an eye out for "no trespassing" signs. He'd rather leave items behind if a property owner or security guard tells him to vacate the premises, he says.
Even Stevens expresses surprise at how much money he's made, saying he doesn't necessarily think his annual income is sustainable. When he "stumbled into" dumpster diving, he was approximately $12,000 in debt after years of poor spending habits fueled partially by a drug addiction, a stark change from his affluent childhood, he says.
"I dug myself out of a hole. I built up my savings. I really did much more than I thought was possible," says Stevens.
Stevens, a Nashville native, is the son of a five-time Grammy Award-winning producer of country and gospel music who has worked with artists like Blake Shelton and Carrie Underwood. His life took a turn in college when he developed an addiction to prescription Adderall, leading him to drop out partway through his senior year in 2018, he says.
His lack of a college degree made landing full-time work a challenge. He says his parents can afford to support him financially, and they've done so in specific emergency occasions. But mostly, his father wants his kids to learn to fend for themselves, he says: "He will let me sit on the coals for the sake of learning how to swim. That's taught me a lot [and] given me a lot of valuable skills and a tough mentality."
Unemployed, Stevens started combing through thrift shops and Goodwill clothing racks for vintage apparel to sell on eBay. He was inspired by YouTube influencers like Rick Senko, he says, whose Fort Lauderdale, Florida-based clothing resale business Technsports brought in $6.5 million in annual revenue as recently as 2024.
But Stevens' returns were inconsistent, and he often spent his profits on drugs or luxury shopping sprees, he says. After his parents funded a rehab stint in 2021 — helping him "quit doing the hard drugs," he says — he spent his money chasing other dopamine hits. Those indulgences included a $1,200 pair of Christian Dior Birkenstock sandals, an 85-inch flat-screen television and a $30,000 down payment on a Mercedes-AMG sedan that he later lost because he couldn't afford the total cost, he says.
By June 2023, he could no longer afford to pay rent, so he lived in a rented storage unit until the business's security found and evicted him, and then stayed in his Nissan Sentra for three weeks, he says. Homelessness shocked him into learning to manage his "reckless" spending habits, he says: "Being punished by your own spending addiction was a wringer that I promised myself I can't be put through again."
In October 2023, a cousin lent him money to start renting an apartment, and Stevens worked to stick to a sensible enough budget for his thrifting income to cover future rent and basic expenses, he says. Five months later, he found a discarded pair of black Nike Air Force Ones in good condition next to a gas station pump. He took them home, sanitized them and sold them online for $35, he says.
"That was the first time I had ever found something that was trash and sold it and made a little bit of money," says Stevens.
Once he started dumpster diving, Stevens was hooked "because I never stopped finding good stuff in these dumpsters," he says.
His biggest score to date: dozens of discarded Steelcase office chairs, worth $1,000-plus each when new, outside an overflowing office park dumpster, he says. He got his car — by this point, a used pickup truck and a self-built trailer — and hauled away 190 chairs to list online at hundreds of dollars apiece. He sold the majority of them in bulk transactions on Facebook Marketplace for $17,000, and brought in an additional $10,600 selling the remaining chairs individually, documents show.
If Stevens manages to find roughly one valuable haul per month, he can fill his $400-a-month storage unit and start listing the items. For the most part, he scopes out corporate environments, preferring "dry dumpsters" over ones laden with food waste, he says. Office trash is particularly profitable when companies downsize, says Stevens: Once, he found 120 standing desks discarded outside a building.
Near high-end apartment buildings, Stevens has found furniture from brands like West Elm, iPads, electronics and power tools in working condition, he says. "Almost every piece of furniture in my apartment came from a dumpster," says Stevens.
Stevens works alone and minimizes gas costs by sticking to locations within a few miles from his apartment. The majority of his income has come from big hauls across his five highest-earning months, reflecting the venture's hit-or-miss nature. "I got really lucky earlier this year and I made a ton of money. I'm not acting like this is something I could do every year," he says.
So he saves as much of his earnings as possible, "constantly" talking himself out of unnecessary purchases, he says. And he's studying the business of real estate wholesaling — which involves securing contracts for distressed properties and flipping them to investors for a fee — as a potentially more secure way to earn a living, he adds.
Still, he acknowledges the allure of knowing his next big payday could always be one dumpster away.
"I don't see myself ever turning down a good looking dumpster," says Stevens. "I have found so much cool stuff that I feel like I'll always be curious about what's in that dumpster."

articles.title_orig: Italy's Meloni blames pro-Russian hackers for cyberattack on minister
articles.title_zh: Italy's Meloni blames pro-Russian hackers for cyberattack on minister
articles.content_orig:
MILAN — Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani said Saturday that his personal data had been disseminated on the dark web, an encrypted part of the internet, and that he has been exposed to “threats and intimidation.” Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blamed pro-Russian hackers for the leak.
Tajani made the announcement in a social media post following a string of hoax bomb threats across Europe that caused flight diversions, security threats against broadcasters as well as recent attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions.
“For days, cybercriminals have been spreading my personal data on the dark web and seeking other information, in fact exposing me and my family to new threats and intimidation,” Tajani said, adding that the criminals “are prepared to pay for other details on me and my loved ones.”
Meloni, in a separate statement, expressed solidarity with Tajani “following the revelations about the activities of pro-Russian hackers, and the publication on the dark web of personal data.” She called attempts to sell confidential information about government officials “a matter of grave concern that must be addressed with the utmost determination.”
Tajani, who is also a vice premier in Italy’s government, did not specify what kind of information had been shared, but suggested that the cyberthreat was ongoing.
“I will not allow myself to be intimidated in any way,” Tajani said. “I will continue working to defend my ministry, and Italy, and I will further strengthen the ties and cooperation to protect ourselves together.”
Tajani did not indicate who might be responsible for the cyberattack but reiterated the Italian government’s support for Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: Strait of Hormuz could reopen under Qatari plan to end US war with Iran
articles.title_zh: Strait of Hormuz could reopen under Qatari plan to end US war with Iran
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Qatar has floated a new plan to restore shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and end the conflict between the United States and Iran, despite reports of renewed US strikes on a key Iranian island .
Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, the emir of mediating Qatar, spoke with US president Donald Trump about their vision for a deal to end the eight-month war, Qatari media reported on Friday.
Al-Thani said on Saturday that the Trump administration was willing to find a solution after the midterm elections, which produced a damning verdict of the conflict and its impact on fuel prices last week.
Under Qatar’s proposal, the US would lift its blockade on Iranian ports and release some of its £6bn worth of frozen Iranian assets, according to the Guardian .
Iran would also agree to visits by IAEA nuclear watchdog inspectors to its main facilities, before reopening the Strait of Hormuz to commercial traffic on the second day, the newspaper said.
Under the Qatari deal, and crucially for Trump, who casus belli was that Iran should never be able to acquire nuclear weapons, the regime would apparently not have to give up its nuclear stockpiles.
The Islamic Republic has made overtures to controlling the vital Strait, through which around a fifth of global oil normally passes, with Oman after the war and could begin charging fees for safe passage.
Under the Qatari deal, Tehran would reopen the route already agreed with Muscat, to be jointly lodged with the International Maritime Organisation (IMO).
Oman’s foreign minister, Badr Albusaidi, has separately spoken with Iran about the future administration of the Strait, including the need to register the proposal with the IMO.
Muscat has its own long-term proposal for the running of the channel, which would only see shipping companies charged for services, not tolls per se.
Iran has also sought to resolve a number of secondary issues thrown by the conflict, which began with US-Israeli strikes on February 28.
Ending the parallel clashes in Lebanon, pulling US forces back from the region and paying war reparations are all new obstacles that will require mediation.
Tehran has been proposing its own seven-day plan to end the war since September, but that has so far been rejected by Trump.
It calls for Washington to lift its blockade, unfreeze assets and approve an Iranian-backed route through the Strait of Hormuz, after which the contested waterway would be reopened.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters on Thursday that Tehran has also submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar.
They said the US was reviewing its but that future discussions would still depend on Washington first meeting Tehran’s seven stated demands.
Ali Bagheri Kani, the deputy head of Iran's top security body, told Iranian state television on Friday that they were still not satisfied with “paper commitments” and must see practical steps from the US.
With diplomatic efforts still on ice, Iranian media on Saturday said it appeared two missiles had struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has repeatedly said it would respond to new attacks by striking at US and Israeli targets in neighboring countries.
The United States has not yet announced any attack on targets inside Iran.

articles.title_orig: New Zealand in political limbo after knife-edge election
articles.title_zh: New Zealand in political limbo after knife-edge election
articles.content_orig:
New Zealand election 'too close to call' - so who's won?
There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show.
Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached.
But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while".
The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment.
Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests, on 5.
New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon addressed supporters in Auckland as votes were being counted
The electoral commission was not due to announce the official result until 27 November.
Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you".
He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations."
Elsewhere, Labour leader Hipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said."
Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground".
More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share.
But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%.
They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests.
New Zealand election 2026: What you need to know
The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side.
It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats.
Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground."
Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern".
"It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said.
Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas.
The Greens â who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops â saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points.
Labour Party leader Chris Hipkins speaking to supporters
Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders
"Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said.
More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia.
New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions.
Each voter makes two choices â for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.title_zh: Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes
articles.content_orig:
Moscow used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in attacks on electricity substations and bridge over the Dnipro
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River.
Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles.
Negotiators from Russia , Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war.
Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said .
Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl.
The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines.
The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime.
They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN , Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe.
In a series of social media posts , Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed.
after newsletter promotion
Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined.
Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.”
Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato.
Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.
